*Early Life*
Raymond III was born around 1140 to Raymond II Count of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem daughter of King Baldwin II. When his father was assassinated in 1152 the young boy became the new count. Due to his minority he was placed under the guardianship of the king of Jerusalem. He was later handed over to Nur ad-Din as a hostage and spent his formative years in Damascus. This unique experience gave him fluency in Arabic and insight into the politics of his Muslim neighbors.

*Political Career and Regency*
Upon his return to Tripoli Raymond emerged as one of the most capable statesmen in the Crusader states. When King Baldwin IV came of age Raymond maintained close ties to the royal court. In 1174 he had served as regent during Baldwin's minority. He was again appointed regent when Baldwin V became king in 1185. Following Baldwin V's death in 1186 Raymond sought to secure the succession through Isabella. He arranged her marriage to Humphrey IV of Toron hoping to limit Lusignan influence. However political pressure forced Raymond to accept the coronation of Guy of Lusignan. In response Raymond withdrew to Tripoli and refused to cooperate with the new king.

*Battle of Hattin and Death*
In summer 1187 Guy led the kingdom's army to relieve the siege of Tiberias. Raymond opposed the campaign but was overruled. At the Battle of Hattin the Crusader army was encircled and destroyed. Contemporary accounts differ on Raymond's role. Some say he broke through Saladin's lines early in the battle. Others accuse him of cowardice. After the defeat Raymond retreated to Tripoli. He died in late 1187 possibly in September. His death was followed by the fall of the County of Tripoli to Saladin in the following years.

*Legacy*
Raymond III occupies a controversial place in Crusader history. Modern historians often view him as a pragmatic leader who tried to negotiate with Saladin to preserve the Holy Land. However his enemies accused him of treachery for his role at Hattin. His death in 1187 marked the end of effective resistance in the County of Tripoli. Within five years Saladin had captured the major cities of the county. Raymond's story illustrates the difficult choices faced by Crusader leaders in the late twelfth century.

A MOST HUMBLE ITINERARY FOR ONE BOUND FOR THE LAND OF THE RISING SUN

Most gracious wanderer! Prithee take thou this humble travel plan penned in the manner of the Bard of Avon. May it serve thee well upon thy journey through the mystic lands of Nippon.

Prologue
Hark noble wanderer and lend thine ear
To this our humble script of travels far
Where cherry blossoms fall and temples cheer
And bullet trains do fly like a shooting star.

Act the First — In Tokyo the Modern
Day the First:
Thou shalt descend at Haneda's gate by night
Where neon signs do gild the darkened sky
Take rest thy weary bones till morning light
For Tokyo's fair wonders wait thee nigh.

Day the Second:
At Tsukiji market feast on tuna bright
Then unto Senso-ji's most ancient shrine
Where incense curls and prayers do take their flight
And Asakusa's bells in chorus chime.

Day the Third:
By shinkansen to Hakone make thy way
Where Mount Fuji her snowy peak reveals
In onsen waters wash thy cares away
Beneath the moon where firefly light steals.

Act the Second — In Kyoto the Ancient
Day the Fourth:
By bullet train to Kyoto take thy flight
Where geishas glide through Gion's lantern lanes
In ryokan rest where hosts do treat thee right
And tatami mats do soothe thy travel pains.

Day the Fifth:
Through Fushimi Inari's thousand torii gates
Where foxes guard the path to sacred peak
Then unto Kinkaku-ji where gold awaits
A golden pavilion for thee to seek.

Day the Sixth:
To Nara take the train where deer do roam
And bow before the great Daibutsu's might
This bronze Buddha in his temple home
Shall fill thy soul with wonder and delight.

Act the Third — In Osaka the Merry
Day the Seventh:
To Osaka go where merchants loud do call
Where neon lights do pierce the velvet night
In Dotonbori feast on dishes all
And try the takoyaki burning bright.

Act the Fourth — The Farewell
Day the Eighth:
Return to Tokyo or take thy flight
With memories stored within thy beating heart
Of temples shrines and cherry blossoms bright
'Twas but a glimpse of Japan's fairest art.

Epilogue
Farewell dear traveller and may the gods
Of travel smile upon thy path ahead
With memories made on these most blessed sods
Where ancient meets the modern newly wed.
